Three days after the Republican Party lost at least forty-four House seats and seven Senate seats, the president named Stephen Miller White House chief of staff. Miller is the central architect of the administration's immigration actions across both terms: the zero-tolerance border policy of 2018, travel restrictions on several Muslim-majority nations, and an executive push directing Immigration and Customs Enforcement to arrest 3,000 people a day, backed by about 170 billion dollars under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Ask who bears the cost of that structure and who was asked. A Fox News exit survey found 58 percent of voters believed federal immigration enforcement had gone too far. The voters answered on Tuesday. The appointment came on Friday.

We think the question is not Miller's character but what the office now rewards. Republican critics and business sectors have already expressed concern about his focus on hardline enforcement after the results. The incoming House majority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, urged the president to reverse the appointment. The Daily Beast reported lobbying calls by Katie Miller urging allies to back her husband; the Associated Press and RTE did not address that account.

A chief of staff decides who reaches the president. On Monday, the person most identified with the policy a majority of voters rejected will hold that door. The Congress that meets him in January is one his party no longer controls. That is the check the structure left standing.
